Three experimental questions matter most. First, whether the replay selection criteria are meaningful: trajectories with high visual dependency and low entropy should outperform naive replay or reward-only replay. Second, whether token-level advantage allocation improves over uniform sequence-level credit assignment, length-normalized variants, or simpler token masks. Third, whether the two modules are complementary: replay-only, token-allocation-only, and full PIVOT should show that trajectory reuse and token credit assignment address different bottlenecks.

The limitations matter: the reasoning judge is not validated against human moral judgments, and the custom scenario annotations have no formal inter-annotator agreement.df:T8ce,The method has three core pieces. First, a unified parameter space. Instead of maintaining separate generator and solver models, the authors use one base model, switched by role-specific system prompts into a Scaffolder or a Learner. The Scaffolder proposes new tasks conditioned on historical outcomes, and the Learner attempts them in an external environment. The motivation is straightforward: if both roles share weights, improvements acquired by the Learner through RL can directly improve the Scaffolder’s ability to place tasks at the right difficulty.

Second, difficulty alignment through the so-called Stretch Zone. The paper does not optimize for “harder is better.” It tries to jointly satisfy task validity, learnability, and behavioral stability. In the formulation, a domain verifier provides a validity signal, a difficulty reward favors tasks near the Learner’s boundary, and a replay term reinforces likelihood on verified successful trajectories. This trade-off matters. If the generator only pushes difficulty upward, it can drift into unsolvable regions. If training only replays successful trajectories, it collapses back into the comfort zone.

Third, an alternating dual-loop update scheme. One loop updates the Scaffolder for difficulty alignment; the other updates the Learner for task solving. The implementation is not a single differentiable end-to-end loss. The Scaffolder generates adaptive constraints from historical feedback, such as bargaining bottom lines or resource constraints in optimization tasks. After verifier filtering, these tasks are passed to the Learner, which is optimized with a GRPO-style group-relative reward objective. At the end of each epoch, verified successful trajectories are replayed with an SFT-style objective to stabilize behavior and reduce drift.

Relative to prior work, the main differences are clear. It does not rely on a frozen environment generator. It is not a teacher-student pipeline. It is not standard curriculum learning with a manually scheduled difficulty ladder. And it is not classic two-agent self-play with fully separate models. The design is closer to role switching inside one model than to conventional co-evolution between two independently trained agents.e0:T5df,The evaluation spans two very different constrained-reasoning settings: multi-turn bargaining and mathematical/operations-research style optimization. The bargaining setup uses Craigslist, while the optimization side uses Mano Complex and Complex OR. The main empirical findings are threefold. First, STRETCH breaks early training plateaus that static RL baselines hit quickly. Second, it outperforms domain-specific baselines on both domains in final task success or score, suggesting the gains are not tied to one verifier or one reward design. Third, the ablations support the claimed mechanism: removing dynamic difficulty alignment causes the system to regress toward easy repeated tasks; removing replay makes training less stable and increases forgetting; separating Scaffolder and Learner into different models hurts difficulty calibration and sample efficiency.

From a pretraining perspective, the experimental scope is still limited. These are controlled post-training environments, not large-scale open-domain language modeling runs. The paper emphasizes training dynamics, plateau breaking, and cross-domain transfer more than parameter count, token budget, or scaling behavior. To assess how far the idea transfers to foundation-model training, one would want larger models, longer runs, and more open-ended task distributions.e1:T460,For a quick pass, focus on three places. First, the introduction and the figure defining Comfort, Stretch, and Difficulty zones. That framing drives the whole method. Second, the main training diagram and the alternating update procedure. The key question is why the authors insist on one shared parameter space instead of two models. Third, the ablations, especially the variants without difficulty alignment, without replay, and with separated parameter spaces. Those are the sections that tell you whether this is more than repackaged curriculum RL.

A practical reading order is: problem setup, training loop, then ablations. In about 30 to 45 minutes, that is enough to capture the main idea. Two points deserve deeper inspection. One is how the difficulty reward estimates the capability boundary and how task-specific that estimate is. The other is whether unified role switching creates interference, where the model’s task-generation preferences and task-solving policy contaminate each other. Those issues would become central if one tried to move this idea into pretraining or self-generated data pipelines.e2:T628,The method is Distribution-aware Language Neuron selection (DLN). For each MLP neuron in an autoregressive Transformer with GLU feed-forward blocks, the authors collect continuous activation values for each language instead of reducing them to a binary active/inactive statistic. They then estimate per-language activation distributions and compute pairwise overlap coefficients between languages. Small overlap means the neuron separates those languages well. The resulting pairwise structure is clustered to recover language groupings.

This leads to two neuron types. Single-language neurons (SLNs) are neurons whose activation distribution for one language is separated from the rest. Multi-language neurons (MLNs) are neurons that support a cluster of languages that are similar to each other but separated from other languages. This is a broader and more faithful definition than entropy over positive activation rates, because it captures cases where all languages are mostly positive but occupy different regions, and cases where the informative regime is negative.

A useful detail is the intervention site. The paper evaluates both the usual gate activation site and the gate-up product site, the latter being closer to the effective contribution written back to the residual stream in GLU blocks. Baselines based on activation probability degrade substantially there, while DLN remains selective. The main innovation is therefore not a heavy model component, but a better neuron selection criterion built on continuous distributions and pairwise language relations.e3:T4dc,Main experiments are conducted on Llama-3.1-8B and SmolLM3-3B-Base using two held-out corpora, with three additional models in the appendix. The key evaluation is causal ablation rather than correlation-style probing: remove selected neurons and measure target-language damage versus collateral damage on other languages.

For SLNs, DLN yields up to 4.9x higher on-target language damage per neuron while preserving off-target performance better than activation-probability baselines. This suggests the selected neurons are more causally specific rather than merely important in a generic sense. For MLNs, DLN uncovers shared structures such as a Chinese–Japanese coalition, producing 7.12x greater within-cluster damage while using 2.1x fewer neurons.

Two analyses stand out. First, DLN finds English SLNs in the negative activation regime that are invisible to positive-rate metrics but still act as functional triggers for language control. Second, DLN remains effective at the gate-up product site, where baseline methods lose much of their selectivity. The strongest evidence in the paper is not an average benchmark gain, but improved causal selectivity: fewer neurons, stronger target-specific effects, and less off-target disruption.e4:T4d7,Two-layer contribution:
- Theory (MUtE*): define erasure as a map f: R^D→R^D producing Q=f(X) such that concept information is removed (perfect privacy / indistinguishability across class-conditionals in the erased space) while utility is maximized (minimal distortion / maximal retained information under the chosen criterion). The authors characterize optimal erasure functions and show that optimality inherently induces a dual deterministic counterfactual mapping between concept classes.
- Practice (MUtE): to avoid the heavy compute of general nonlinear erasure (adversarial training, density estimation, Bayesian optimization), they propose an implementation with a translational bias: many concepts in modern encoders behave approximately like linear directions / translations, so counterfactual trajectories can be parameterized as (near) translations. This yields an efficient procedure that supports both erasure and counterfactual representation generation.
Compared to projection-based linear methods (INLP/LEACE), MUtE expands the objective to a more general optimality framing and explicitly couples erasure with counterfactuals; computationally, it trades generality for scalability via a structured geometric assumption.e5:T605,The method is straightforward. For each trained model, the authors extract WeightWatcher metrics from layer weight matrices, focusing on quantities such as stable rank and log α-norm, alongside more conventional measures of generalization. The theoretical backdrop is heavy-tailed self-regularization, where well-trained networks are expected to deviate from random-matrix behavior and exhibit structured empirical spectral densities. WeightWatcher summarizes this structure through power-law fits and norm-based statistics.

The empirical protocol then compares these spectral metrics against actual MIA vulnerability measured by attacks such as LiRA. The analysis separates overall attack success from performance in the low-false-positive-rate regime, which matters more for practical auditing. The main finding is that stable rank is strongly positively correlated with overall MIA success, while log α-norm is consistently negatively correlated with attack success in the low-FPR regime. The paper also shows that spectral metrics and generalization gap are not redundant: combining them improves prediction of whether a model should be considered high risk.

A useful nuance from the full paper is that the authors do not claim spectral metrics explain privacy leakage mechanistically. Their position is more modest. These metrics appear to capture aspects of internal organization that are missed by train-test gap alone, but the work stops short of linking layerwise spectral evolution to sample-level memorization in a causal way.e6:T58b,The experiments are conducted on image and tabular classification models rather than language models, which is an important limitation. Across multiple datasets and model settings, the paper compares WeightWatcher metrics, generalization gap, and measured MIA leakage. Three results stand out.

First, stable rank is a stronger predictor of overall MIA success than generalization gap across the evaluated settings. This matters if the goal is coarse screening of which trained models are more likely to leak membership information.

Second, in the low-FPR regime, log α-norm is a more consistent predictor than generalization gap. That is a practically relevant result because privacy auditing usually cares about low false-positive operation.

Third, spectral metrics and generalization gap provide complementary information. A combined predictor performs better at identifying high-risk models than either signal alone. The paper also notes that not all WeightWatcher metrics are equally useful; stable rank and log α-norm are the most reliable among those tested.

The practical advantage is computational: unlike LiRA or RMIA, the proposed proxy only needs access to trained weights. The limitations are equally clear: no Transformer or LLM experiments, no large-scale pretraining setting, and no evidence yet that the correlations remain stable across optimizer choices, training scales, or distribution shifts.e7:T414,For a skim, start with the introduction and background to understand what is being replaced: expensive shadow-model-based privacy auditing, not privacy evaluation as a whole. The argument revolves around three objects: a moral subspace, a refusal direction, and a moral-judgment direction.

The moral subspace is built from three independent moral-content sources: Moral Stories, Understanding Fables, and ETHICS. For each source, the authors compute a moral-versus-neutral mean-difference direction, then orthonormalize the resulting set into an effective rank-3 subspace. This design choice is important. The goal is not simply to maximize dimensionality, but to obtain a construct-diverse, source-distinguishable representation that is less vulnerable to single-dataset contamination.

The refusal direction is extracted in the standard representation-reading style from the mean difference between refused and complied requests. A judgment direction is defined analogously for moral judgment. The authors then examine how these directions relate to the moral subspace across layers and positions, with special attention to the decision site: the assistant header or end-of-prompt control token where the refusal gate is read out.

A major strength of the paper is that OLMo-3 provides both base and post-training checkpoints, allowing the authors to track representational formation over training stages. They report that the moral subspace is already present in pretraining and remains nearly the same object through the final model, with a checkpoint-to-final cosine of 0.999. Post-training mainly rotates it once, by about 40 degrees, rather than rebuilding it. By contrast, the refusal gate has only a weak precursor in pretraining: proto-refusal-to-gate cosine is 0.155, about twice the matched null but still far from a mature gate. This asymmetry supports the paper’s central distinction between deep comprehension and shallow control.

The next step is geometric analysis at the decision site. Across four models, the control token is an 8-to-15 dimensional bottleneck. Within that bottleneck, the refusal-decision direction is largely separated from the moral-judgment direction. On OLMo, refusal projects only 0.10 of its norm onto the moral subspace, with mean absolute cosine around 0.06, below the moral-family band. This suggests that refusal is not broadly reading the moral subspace where comprehension lives.

The strongest evidence comes from a nested interchange rank sweep on OLMo. The authors progressively expand the rank of the patched moral basis and compare how refusal coupling and judgment coupling respond. If refusal depended on broad moral content, its transferred effect should keep increasing with rank. Instead, judgment coupling rises with rank and reconstructs about 0.66 of the subspace patch effect, while refusal coupling quickly saturates at the rank-1 harm level. That is the key causal result behind the title: refusal reads only a slice of what the model knows.

Finally, the four-model panel is interpreted along two separate axes: what refusal reads, and how the model commits. Some models appear to read harm, some broader moral content, and commitment can happen at the read layer, earlier than the read layer, or remain reversible under later deliberation. This decomposition is more informative than a single scalar notion of alignment depth.ec:T816,There are three experimental blocks that carry most of the paper.

If time is tight, prioritize the OLMo causal interchange over the broader four-model geometric panel.ee:T725,The paper compares three state structures under a shared setup. Frontier superposition stores only the active alternatives at the current step. Cumulative superposition stores the full reached history. General weighted superposition allows arbitrary weight allocation over that history. All three use the same graph, candidate bank, downstream query family, and decoder, so the comparison isolates only one design choice: what the continuous state preserves.

The theoretical core is a critical-dimension analysis. Objects receive independent Gaussian embeddings, and the latent state is a normalized superposition of those embeddings. A common decoder then tries to distinguish a useful direction from competing directions. The authors derive an exact finite-dimensional score law and use it to compare the minimum hidden dimension needed for reliable decoding. The main result is that for a broad class of state-independent, nonlocalized, bounded-influence queries, cumulative superposition benefits from coherent reinforcement among historically useful components, while unrelated components behave mostly as random interference. So even though cumulative states have larger support, the signal relevant to future computation can be stronger rather than weaker.

The paper then maps this abstraction back to Transformer mechanics. Attention expands the current computation, while residual writing determines whether previous objects are discarded or preserved. In weighted superpositions, the weakest retained coefficient becomes the routing bottleneck: if some historical items receive too little weight, later attention cannot reliably reuse them. This leads to a minimax design principle: when future queries are unknown, uniform cumulative weighting is robustly near-optimal, and in the formal setup it is exactly minimax.ef:T4e1,The experiments are structured to validate the theory rather than to chase a benchmark headline. First, there are controlled simulations checking that the finite-dimensional score law predicts actual retrieval and discrimination behavior. Second, width-scaling experiments compare frontier, cumulative, and weighted superpositions as hidden dimension varies. The central empirical pattern is that cumulative superposition reaches usable performance at smaller widths than frontier superposition for the nonlocalized query classes studied in the theory. Third, the paper implements the attention-residual construction in lightweight models and GPT-2-style token-level settings to test the mechanism-level claim that the weakest retained coefficient is the practical routing bottleneck.

Two aspects are especially useful. One, the cumulative advantage is not restricted to trivial symmetric or purely additive queries; the query family is allowed to be continuous, correlated, asymmetric, and identity-dependent. Two, the failure mode of weighted superposition is interpretable: the problem is not simply insufficient total energy, but poor allocation, where potentially useful historical items are assigned coefficients too small to be reused later.f0:T4b0,Start with the setup and the definitions of the three superposition structures. Data come from filtered EPITOME peer-support dialogues, with short seeker posts and self-harm-related cases removed to reduce context sparsity and safety-template confounds. For each empathy mechanism, the authors build contrastive sets and extract steering vectors from residual-stream activations.

The main intervention is contrastive activation addition: a direction is estimated from activation differences between higher-scoring and lower-scoring examples for a given mechanism, then added at inference time to a chosen layer. The contribution is less about inventing a new steering algorithm and more about the analysis stack built around it.

There are three key components. First, a layer sweep identifies where interventions are stable across models; middle layers emerge as the most reliable, with layer 15 receiving special attention in the analysis. Second, target versus off-target evaluation measures not only whether ER steering raises ER, but also whether it unintentionally shifts IP and EX, and likewise for the other directions. This tests separability rather than raw controllability. Third, geometric and projection analyses examine pairwise structure among ER/IP/EX directions and quantify how much persona-induced activation movement lies inside the recovered mechanism subspace.

Compared with prior activation-steering work on honesty, refusal, or sycophancy, the difference is substantial. The target behavior here is inherently multi-component. The authors use steering as a representational probe, not just a control knob. And they explicitly test whether prompt-induced persona effects align with the recovered mechanism basis, which is a deeper question than simply comparing response scores under different personas.f3:T700,The experiments support three main findings. First, steering is feasible. Across all three models, contrastive activation addition at middle layers consistently shifts EPITOME proxy scores in the intended direction. The trend survives evaluation with a second automated judge, which reduces the chance that the result is only an artifact of one classifier. The paper also reports partial out-of-domain transfer, suggesting the vectors are not purely dataset-specific surface heuristics.

Second, the three empathy mechanisms are not independently controllable. Steering along one recovered direction improves the target mechanism, but also causes measurable off-target changes in the other two. The result is not that ER, IP, and EX are indistinguishable; rather, they are distinguishable but share representational structure strongly enough that clean disentanglement fails. This is the central empirical basis for the paper’s “multi-axial” claim.

Third, persona effects mostly fall outside the recovered mechanism basis. Persona prompts can produce large changes in output-level empathy scores, yet the corresponding activation shifts project only weakly onto the ER/IP/EX subspace. The headline number is that at layer 15, the recovered ER/IP/EX basis explains only about 3% of the persona-induced mean-squared activation-shift magnitude. That is a strong indication that persona-conditioned empathy variation is not just movement along “more ER,” “more IP,” or “more EX,” but involves broader representational changes.

All experiments are on 7B–8B instruction-tuned models. Evaluation relies mainly on EPITOME classifiers plus an LLM judge, so the findings are best read as robust mechanism-level evidence rather than a final statement about human-perceived empathy.f4:T48c,For a skim, start with the two research questions in the introduction, then jump to the method figure and the layer-sweep results. In residual space, Δ is the sub-layer residual update and z is the sub-layer input (or block input for block-level updates). In attention value space, Δ is the pre-output-projection value aggregation, decomposed relative to the token’s own value vector; this separates self-value flow from cross-token aggregation effects.

Causality is tested via component-scaling interventions: multiply either Δ_parallel or Δ_perp by a scalar and measure behavioral degradation. The key empirical asymmetry is consistent across models and layers: scaling Δ_perp is highly disruptive, while scaling Δ_parallel is comparatively benign over a wide range—especially in value space for cross-token aggregation.

The paper then extends the geometry to two applied settings:
- Compression: decompose quantization/pruning-induced update distortion into parallel vs perpendicular error; perpendicular error is more predictive of final quality.
- Pretraining: introduce parallel attention suppression (residual-space and value-space variants). The motivation is to discourage learning direction-preserving attention components that appear behaviorally redundant, potentially reallocating capacity toward direction-changing updates and stabilizing optimization.f6:Ta28,文章的技术路线是把每一种失败模式都拆成四步：先展示最初看起来像发现的现象，再指出暴露问题的 tell，再给出修复协议，最后用独立控制验证修复是否有效。贯穿全文的主线是四条纪律：第一，用 positive-control ladder 校准仪器，确认它在目标位置真的有区分能力；第二，用 orthogonal cell 做认证，避免同一类测量自证；第三，在花算力做 patch 或大规模干预前先算 power；第四，所有“reads X”结论都必须相对模型 commit 深度来陈述。

文中一个关键背景是 decision site 的低维瓶颈。作者用 participation ratio 估计残差流协方差的有效维度，发现四个模型在控制 token 处只有约 8 到 15 维，而同层内容 token 位置仍是 33 到 40+ 的健康高维。这个事实解释了为什么 projection-fraction instrument 会失灵：在一个只有十来个有效自由度的通道里，正控方向投到自身 span 的比例可能并不比随机方向高，导致“低投影”不能说明缺失，只能说明仪器没分辨率。

六个 failure mode 里，较有方法学含金量的几个是：
1. 对 projection fraction，作者要求先做 band/below-null 检查和正控梯度，只有当正控在该位置能明显高于 null，投影读数才可解释。
2. 对 covariance-matched null，作者指出在 massive-activation family 中，匹配协方差会让几乎所有方向都显得“典型”，null 失去对比度，因此需要额外的 family-aware 控制，而不是只看协方差匹配。
3. 对 per-head OV attribution，作者发现 reordered-normalization 架构里按 head 估计的写入量会比真实 residual write 高约三倍，因此不能把 OV 路径贡献直接当作残差写入，需要用真实残差差分或更接近执行图的估计来校正。
4. 对 interchange patch，作者强调如果 outcome 已经贴近 ceiling，engage/disengage 两个方向会因为 operating point 不对称而出现 sign-chaotic；修复方式是把结论写成 depth- and operating-point-referenced，并在非饱和区间做验证。
5. 对 read-from verdict，作者要求把测量层和 commit 层分开：如果模型在更早层已经决定，晚层读到的相关性可能只是决策后的回声，而不是因果读取。

整体上，这不是提出单一新算法，而是把 interpretability instrument 当成实验仪器来做校准学。它和很多 mechanistic interpretability 文章最大的区别，是作者不急着给机制故事，而是先给失效边界和可复现 protocol。f7:Tb2f,The paper is organized instrument by instrument. For each failure mode, it follows the same pattern: show the initial apparent finding, identify the tell that exposed the failure, propose a repair protocol, and certify the repair with an orthogonal control. Four procedural rules run through the whole note: calibrate against a positive-control ladder, certify with an orthogonal cell, compute statistical power before spending compute on interventions, and state every read-from claim relative to the model’s commitment depth.

A key empirical backdrop is the low-dimensional decision-site bottleneck. The authors estimate effective dimensionality with the participation ratio of the residual-stream covariance and find that the control token sits in an 8-to-15 dimensional channel across four models, while content positions at comparable layers remain much higher-rank. This observation explains one of the main instrument failures: in such a narrow channel, a projection-fraction metric can lose discriminative power exactly where the interesting directions live, so a low projection score may reflect instrument weakness rather than representational absence.

Among the six failure modes, several stand out as broadly reusable methodology:
1. For projection-based instruments, the protocol requires checking whether the positive control is actually above the null band at the target position. If the instrument cannot separate its own positive control from null, the projection number is not interpretable.
2. For covariance-matched nulls, the paper shows that in massive-activation families the null can saturate until nearly every direction looks typical. Matching covariance alone is therefore insufficient; one needs family-aware controls or additional diagnostics.
3. For per-head OV attribution, the authors show that reordered-normalization architectures can induce about a 3x overestimate relative to the true residual write. The fix is to ground attribution in actual residual differences or a closer execution-level estimator, rather than treating OV-path attribution as the write itself.
4. For interchange patching, they show that operating-point asymmetry matters. When one arm is near ceiling, engage/disengage interventions can become sign-chaotic. The remedy is to report effects relative to operating point and verify them away from saturation.
5. For read-from claims, the paper separates the read layer from the commitment layer. If the model has already committed earlier, a later-layer correlation may be a post-decision echo rather than a causal read.

The paper’s distinctive move is to treat interpretability tools as laboratory instruments that require calibration, power analysis, and certification. It is much less interested in a mechanism narrative than in the validity conditions under which such a narrative can be trusted.f8:T5bd,The most important quantitative result is the decision-site bottleneck itself. The participation ratio at the control token is reported as 14.7 for OLMo-3-7B-Instruct, 8.6 for Qwen2.5-7B, 10.2 for Llama-3.1-8B, and roughly 9.4 raw / 12.8 standardized for GPT-OSS-20B at its relevant decision token. These values are only 4% to 8% of their column-shuffle references, indicating a strong compression rather than a mild reduction in rank. By contrast, content positions at similar layers remain in the 33+ to 40+ range, supporting the claim that the bottleneck is localized to the decision site.

The paper is not benchmark-driven. Its empirical contribution is a set of quantified diagnostic failures. The headline numbers matter because they are large enough to reverse conclusions: per-head OV attribution can overshoot true residual writes by about threefold on reordered-norm models; covariance-matched nulls can saturate so badly that every direction appears typical; read-from verdicts can become artifacts when measured after commitment. These are not small calibration errors but systematic distortions.

Another useful aspect of the experimental presentation is that the authors do not overclaim universality. Coverage differs by failure mode, and not every protocol is established on all four models. That restraint is a strength: the note presents portable procedures tested within a concrete program, not a blanket claim that every failure appears everywhere.f9:T8ae,论文沿用 datamodeling 设定：用连续权重 w 给每个训练样本加权，训练算法 A（含优化器、LR schedule、随机性固定）把 w 映射到最终参数 θ(w)，每个测试查询 q 的标量测量 φ_q(θ)（常见是 loss）与训练权重的导数 ∂f_q/∂w_i 就是“样本 i 对查询 q 的影响”。把所有查询与所有训练样本的影响堆成影响矩阵（Jacobian）J∈R^{k×n}。

核心重述是：MAGIC 能给出 J 的某一行（固定 q，对所有训练样本的影响）或某些向量-雅可比积/雅可比-向量积，但若要对每个 q 都跑一次反传穿越训练轨迹，成本随 k 线性爆炸。作者把“预算受限的多查询归因”表述为：在只能获得少量对 J 的线性测量（left/right vector products）的情况下，估计整个大矩阵。

论文区分了两个目标，并指出它们对应不同的最优测量策略：
1) reconstruction：尽量在 Frobenius 意义下重建 J（更偏向把大行范数的查询重建得更好）；
2) attribution：更像“每个查询一票”的平均归因质量（不希望被少数大范数查询主导）。作者强调这两者的差异不是表述细节，而会改变你应该如何分配测量预算。

在算法上给出两条路线，均建立在现有 metagradient 原语之上：
- Mage（Metagradient Approximation by Gram Eigendirections）：面向 reconstruction。直觉是用少量测量去捕捉影响矩阵的主能量子空间（类似从 Gram 矩阵的特征方向提取主成分），让重建误差主要落在尾部方向。
- Spell（Spherical Estimation for the Linear datamodeling score at Low budgets）：面向 attribution。它更强调对查询方向的“均匀覆盖”，用球面/各向同性的测量设计减少对行范数分布的偏置，从而在低预算下让“平均查询”的归因更稳。

与以往可扩展归因（近似 influence function、tracing、Shapley 近似）相比，这篇工作的关键差别不在于再造一个新的近似公式，而是：以 MAGIC 的精确 metagradient 为底座，把问题提升为“矩阵估计 + 测量设计”，并明确区分‘重建矩阵’与‘做归因评分’两种评价口径。fa:T80a,They adopt the datamodeling setup: assign a continuous weight vector w over training points, run a fixed (randomness-fixed) training algorithm A to get parameters θ(w), and define each test query q as a scalar measurement φ_q(θ) (typically loss). The influence scores are the Jacobian entries ∂f_q/∂w_i, and stacking them yields a large influence matrix J ∈ R^{k×n} (k queries, n training points).

MAGIC-style exact influence can compute influences accurately by differentiating through the entire training trajectory, but doing this per query scales linearly in k. The key reframing is: multi-query attribution becomes an influence-matrix estimation problem from a limited number of linear measurements (left/right vector products obtainable via existing metagradient machinery).

A central conceptual contribution is separating two objectives:
- Reconstruction: recover J well in a global (Frobenius-like) sense, which implicitly prioritizes high-row-norm queries.
- Attribution: optimize attribution quality per query more uniformly, avoiding domination by a few large-norm rows.
They show these objectives imply different optimal measurement designs.

They then propose two estimators built on metagradient primitives:
- Mage (Metagradient Approximation by Gram Eigendirections) targets reconstruction by focusing measurements along dominant eigendirections of an associated Gram structure, effectively capturing the high-energy subspace of J.
- Spell (Spherical Estimation for the Linear datamodeling score at Low budgets) targets attribution by using more isotropic/spherical measurement strategies to improve average-per-query attribution under low budgets.

Compared to prior scalable attribution (approximate influence functions, tracing, Shapley approximations), the novelty is less about a new heuristic approximation and more about (i) treating exact metagradients as measurements, (ii) casting the task as matrix estimation, and (iii) making the reconstruction-vs-attribution distinction operational via different measurement schemes.fb:T959,方法设计很干净。作者不从自然语言任务入手，而是构造一组 edge-emitting HMM，让模型读取由这些 HMM 生成的 token 序列，并预测下一个 token。对于每个时间步，真实 belief state 都可以由 HMM 的转移与发射概率精确算出，因此有了一个外部可监督的、理论上正确的表示目标。

论文的第一步是任务筛选。作者在 40 个具有非平凡 belief 结构的 HMM 上评估六个开源 LLM，只保留那些模型已经能接近最优 next-token 预测的过程。这样做是为了避免 probe 结果被“模型根本没学会这个过程”污染。换句话说，他们不是在问任何 HMM 上都能不能读出 belief state，而是在问：当模型行为上已经接近最优时，内部是否真的形成了对应的状态表示。

第二步是线性 probe。作者从不同层的 residual stream 提取激活，用线性回归去预测 belief state 向量，并报告 R2。这里的关键不是单纯 probe 成功，而是 belief state 的几何结构在多个模型、多个 HMM、多个层位上都能被线性读出，说明这种表示不是高度非线性、零散分布的偶然编码，而更像是残差空间中的一个相对规整子空间。

第三步是因果干预。论文做了两类 intervention：patching 和 steering。patching 可以理解为把某个样本在 belief 子空间上的表示替换成另一个表示，再看输出分布如何变化；steering 则是在该子空间上定向移动激活。作者比较了“替换成正确 belief 点”“替换成无关 belief 点”以及未干预模型的预测质量。若 belief 子空间只是相关但无功能，干预不应系统性改变输出；但实验显示，沿 probe 识别出的子空间做正确干预时，模型预测仍接近未干预水平，而替换成不相关 simplex 点会明显恶化。这说明该子空间对下游 next-token prediction 有因果作用。

理论背景上，作者借用了 computational mechanics。这个框架认为，对一个部分可观测随机过程做最优预测，需要维护能压缩过去并保留未来预测信息的充分统计量；在 HMM 场景下，这个量正是 belief state。论文的贡献不是提出新理论，而是把这个理论从 toy transformer 扩展到现成开源 LLM，并给出可证伪的表示预测、probe 和 intervention 证据链。fc:Ta4a,The setup is clean and theory-driven. Instead of using natural-language tasks with ambiguous latent structure, the authors construct edge-emitting HMMs and feed their emitted token sequences to pretrained LLMs. For every time step, the ground-truth belief state can be computed exactly from the HMM dynamics, so the paper has a precise external target for what the model should represent if it is doing optimal latent-state tracking.

The first step is process selection. The authors evaluate six open-source LLMs on many HMMs and keep 40 with non-trivial belief structure on which the models achieve near-optimal next-token prediction. This is an important choice. They are not asking whether belief states are decodable for arbitrary HMMs; they are asking whether, when the model already behaves close to optimally, the corresponding latent posterior is present in the activations.

The second step is linear probing. Residual-stream activations from different layers are used to predict the belief-state vector with linear probes, and performance is measured with R2. The significance is not merely that a probe works. The belief geometry is linearly recoverable across multiple models, multiple HMMs, and at different depths, which suggests that the representation is organized in a relatively structured subspace rather than being diffusely encoded in a highly nonlinear way.

The third step is causal intervention. The paper uses patching and steering targeted at the probe-identified belief subspace. Roughly, patching replaces the belief-subspace component of one activation with another, while steering moves the activation along directions in that subspace. The authors compare interventions that preserve the correct belief geometry against interventions that substitute an unrelated point on the simplex. If the subspace were merely correlated with prediction, these manipulations should not systematically matter. Instead, interventions aligned with the identified belief state preserve prediction quality near the untampered model, while unrelated substitutions degrade it substantially. That makes the case functional rather than purely correlational.

The theoretical framing comes from computational mechanics. In that view, optimal prediction for a partially observed stochastic process requires tracking a sufficient statistic that compresses the past while preserving predictive information about the future. For HMMs, that statistic is exactly the belief state. The paper’s contribution is to carry this prediction from toy models into pretrained open-source LLMs and test it with both probes and interventions.fd:T744,The study covers six open-source LLMs and 40 HMMs. The headline result is that belief states are linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, with peak probe R2 values ranging from 0.83 to 0.99 depending on the model and process. The best layer is not fixed: for some model–HMM pairs the strongest signal appears relatively early, for others later. That suggests belief-state formation is distributed and architecture-dependent rather than confined to the final layers.

A strong part of the experimental design is the behavioral filter. The authors first verify that the model is already near-optimal on next-token prediction for the selected HMMs, and only then analyze representations. This helps separate “the model never learned the process” from “the model learned it but represents it differently.”

The intervention results are the main functional evidence. When patching or steering within the identified belief subspace in a way that preserves the appropriate belief geometry, the KL divergence to the ground-truth next-token distribution remains on the same order as the untampered model. When the activation is replaced with an unrelated point on the belief simplex, prediction quality drops substantially. The abstract does not list all detailed numbers, but the qualitative pattern is consistent and important: correct manipulations of the belief subspace preserve behavior, incorrect ones damage it.

Another good design choice is the use of HMMs with non-trivial belief structure, rather than processes where the next-token distribution already fully captures the hidden dynamics. The paper also includes a contrasting case, Mess3, where hidden-state dynamics are no richer than the observable predictive distribution. That helps rule out the simpler interpretation that the probe is only reading out shallow token statistics.fe:T4b8,Read this one with a specific question in mind: is the paper showing a real mechanism or just a probe artifact? Start with the introduction and Figure 1 to understand the exact hypothesis: not generic latent-state encoding, but belief-state geometry predicted by computational mechanics. Then read the background section on HMMs and belief states carefully so the probe target is unambiguous.

The most important part of the main text is the experimental design: how the 40 HMMs are selected, why near-optimal behavioral performance is required before probing, where in the residual stream the probes are applied, and what the control conditions are. Without those details, the probe results are easy to overinterpret.

After that, focus on the intervention section. The patching and steering constructions, and the use of KL divergence to the ground-truth next-token distribution as the evaluation metric, are what elevate the paper from representational correlation to something closer to mechanistic evidence. A careful first pass should take about 35–50 minutes. If you care about ICL theory or interpretability, the appendix on HMM selection, controls, and layerwise variation is worth the extra time.ff:T43a,The experiments use Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-4-E4B. Activation analysis uses four depth checkpoints per model: layers 8/16/24/31 for Llama-3.1-8B, 9/18/27/35 for Qwen3-8B, and 28/29/40/41 for Gemma-4-E4B. Each condition uses 100 OpenOrca prompts of roughly 100 to 300 words, with adjacent-key typos applied at up to four positions. The observed on-site rotations are 43 to 56 degrees and decay to below 15% within about 10 downstream tokens. A stacked typo bundle reduces single-position prompt-injection probe TPR by 12.0 percentage points at FPR=1%, and threshold recalibration is not sufficient. Multi-position aggregation reduces localized perturbation loss to at most 0.5 percentage points, but distributed perturbations still cause about a 3.8-point drop even with attention- or max-based aggregation. The KV-cache-forked probe suffix closes about 95% of the single-position gap, leaving a 0.6-point residual, while perturbation-augmented training leaves a 3.7-point residual. An LLM-as-judge check labels 94.6% of clean-perturbed pairs as intent-preserving.100:T4de,The method starts from a residual-stream view of a gated MLP neuron. For a GLU neuron, the model reads from the residual stream through input-side vectors such as w_gate and w_in, and writes back along w_out. The authors compute cosine similarity between the read-side and write-side directions and use this as a functional descriptor. Strongly negative cosine indicates a weakening neuron: when the neuron detects a direction in the residual stream, it tends to write in the opposite direction. Positive cosine corresponds to strengthening-like behavior, with intermediate regions capturing weaker or conditional variants.

A useful part of the setup is the explicit treatment of gated activations. Unlike ReLU neurons, SwiGLU and GEGLU can produce both positive and negative outputs, so activation magnitude alone is not enough to characterize function. A neuron can be “on” in one sense while still writing a suppressive update. The paper then applies this IO taxonomy to nine modern LLMs, examining layerwise distributions of neuron classes, correlations with activation frequency, and causal influence via ablations. This matters because the work does not stop at static weight geometry; it tries to connect geometry to runtime behavior.101:T4a9,There are four main empirical findings. First, the same broad layerwise pattern appears across nine LLMs: early-to-middle layers contain many conditional strengthening neurons, while late layers are enriched with weakening neurons. That suggests the read-write geometry is not random but part of a stable functional organization learned during training. Second, IO functionality correlates strongly with activation frequency. Third, weakening neurons are relatively rare but activate often. Fourth, and most importantly, they have disproportionately large causal influence under ablation. Their effect persists even when their gate value is negative, which argues against simplistic notions of neuron importance based only on positive activation.

From the provided text, the paper’s emphasis is on robust structural patterns and causal trends rather than a single headline metric. The key evidence appears in the layer-distribution plots and ablation figures, especially the ones corresponding to Figs. 2, 3, 5, and 6. This is a mechanistic analysis paper, so the main question is whether the phenomenon is consistent, cross-model, and behaviorally meaningful. The answer appears to be yes.102:T529,The main model is a two-block pre-LayerNorm decoder-only Transformer with width 128, four heads, GELU MLPs of width 4d, and tied embeddings/readout. It is trained full-batch with AdamW for 30,000 steps at learning rate 1e-3 and weight decay 1.0, without a schedule or dropout. Tasks include modular addition and modular division at modulus 47, with partial operand-pair training splits. Memory-dominant checkpoints require training accuracy at least 0.99 and OOD accuracy at most 0.35. Persistent generalization requires three consecutive evaluations with training accuracy at least 0.99 and OOD accuracy at least 0.90. All three residual paths gain OOD utility, but block-0 attention gains relative to its neighboring MLP. Selected degree-two modes account for 67% to 92% of the addition contrast across replacement games. The predicted MLP-memory and attention-generalization handoff is reversed, with -0.331 bits per example at the memory anchor and 0 out of 12 pairs in the predicted direction. Routing onset and global rank collapse are not supported. In the path study, block-1 MLP mediates more of the selected-mode effect than all other tested downstream paths in 12 out of 12 pairs. A prime-width-head factorial finds a head-dimension diagonal at modulus 43 but not at 53, limiting any direct architectural rule.103:T426,The proposed pipeline has four stages: Schema Abstraction, Operation Planning, Operand Binding, and Computation. The authors identify stage boundaries using three complementary tools. Layer-to-layer residual-stream cosine similarity reveals where representations change. Category-specific linear probes test which information is present at which depths. Cross-prompt activation patching checks whether replacing a residual segment causally changes the final answer. The same scaffold is then used to analyze NoOp failures. Patching localizes the corruption to Operation Planning. A per-head Direct Logit Attribution method, anchored on whether heads engage with the distractor, identifies a compact set of attention heads that route distractor information into the operation plan. The heads split into groups that push toward or against the wrong plan. Bidirectional attention scaling provides the causal test: amplifying the anti-wrong-plan heads recovers part of the lost accuracy, while ablating relevant heads damages performance on normally solved examples.104:T5af,There are three technical moves worth noting. First, the authors define a row-associated bilinear operator for each gated-FFN output row and compute its Frobenius norm and singular spectrum exactly, instead of relying on a diagonal approximation. This is important because cross terms between hidden units can be substantial, especially in genomic models, so the diagonal proxy is not reliable for cross-model structural claims. Second, candidate rows are selected from activation-derived high-gain signals rather than from weight magnitude alone, and then compared against same-layer random controls and same-layer top-norm controls. This separates rows that are dynamically amplified from rows that merely look large in parameter space. Third, functional importance is measured through interventions: partial suppression and full ablation, evaluated by changes in the model’s native language-model loss; in one generative genomic case study, nucleotide composition shift is also tracked. For multi-row settings, the paper compares additive response models against richer calibrated and pairwise-interaction models to test whether effects are approximately additive or genuinely circuit-like.

Relative to earlier super-weight papers, the novelty is not another catalog of important parameters. The novelty is the explicit separation between structural descriptors and causal function, tested across a 22-model frozen census spanning text and genomics.105:T778,The empirical core is a causal census over 22 frozen models from text and genomics. As a retrospective calibration step, the authors revisit published super-weight coordinates in Llama-7B, Mistral-7B, and OLMo-7B. The down-projection output row containing the published super weight ranks first within its layer under their row-level proxy, which links the new row-based analysis back to the earlier scalar super-weight phenomenon.

The main findings are fourfold. First, activation-selected high-gain rows are functionally enriched: under both partial suppression and full ablation, they induce larger native-loss changes than five same-layer controls. Second, this enrichment is not a calibrated predictor. Signed full-ablation effects vary widely, from negligible or even negative changes to several-hundred-percent increases in native loss. So the candidate set contains both genuinely critical rows and structurally conspicuous but functionally weak ones. Third, neither leading spectral concentration q1 nor operator magnitude predicts the signed full-ablation effect within an architecture class, and the highest-norm rows in the same layer are often causally close to inert. This directly argues against a simple “bigger or sharper means more important” picture. Fourth, the case studies show qualitatively different causal organizations: DNABERT-2 exhibits a robust pretrained pair interaction, suggesting nontrivial circuit dependence, while in GENERator the disruption of a spectrally concentrated row produces a native-loss phenotype mediated mostly at the beginning-of-sequence position, together with a nucleotide-composition shift that tracks damage magnitude and does not require the row’s learned direction.

The paper is careful about effect distributions, controls, and failure cases rather than headline benchmark gains. That makes the conclusions more mechanistic and more trustworthy.106:T4af,Start with the framing in the introduction: the paper deliberately shifts the question from detecting extreme parameters to testing whether structural extremeness transfers as mechanism. Then read the section defining the bilinear operator and the exact computation of norm and spectral concentration; this is where the paper earns its main methodological claim, especially the argument that cross terms matter in genomic models. After that, focus on the 22-model census results and the two case studies: the DNABERT-2 pair interaction and the GENERator beginning-of-sequence mediated damage pattern.

If reading selectively, prioritize the calibration figure around the known Llama/Mistral/OLMo super weights, the main census table or figure comparing candidates against same-layer controls, and the multi-row response-model analysis. Around 25–35 minutes should be enough to extract the main message. The deeper questions left open are also useful: how stable is activation-based candidate discovery across prompts or data slices, and how much of this row-level phenomenon is shaped by training dynamics, optimizer noise, token statistics, or positional structure rather than architecture alone.107:T468,A controlled ablation study rather than a new algorithm:
- Benchmarks: TheAgentCompany (software-company roles, cross-application workflows, coworkers) and APEX-Agents (investment banking, consulting, corporate law; document-heavy analysis/editing).
- Models: Opus-4.8 and GPT-5.5.
- Five interfaces:
  1) Tool-only (typed catalog only)
  2) Bash+Tool (shell + typed catalog)
  3) Bash (shell only)
  4) Bash+Synthesis (shell + persistent workspace; prompts encourage agent-synthesized reusable tools)
  5) PTC (programmatic tool calling): model writes a restricted Python program that can loop/parallelize but can only act through the typed catalog (no shell).
- Controls: same base prompt, task text, and stopping criteria; only interface-specific prompting changes.
- Engineering to reduce confounds: build a 60-tool typed catalog for TheAgentCompany (which lacks an LLM-facing catalog) and patch coworker reliability issues uniformly across interfaces.
- Measurements: task score/pass rate, total tokens and estimated cost, tool-call counts/tokens, call success rate, repetition, plus domain breakdowns and failure analysis.108:T7c1,The method has three main layers. First is purely online orchestration. The system starts from the raw video file and the query. It does not build a query-agnostic memory, does not parse the whole video into a database upfront, and does not rely on a fixed segmentation-and-sampling stage. The agent reasons step by step and invokes tools only when needed. The motivation is straightforward: in long videos, relevant evidence is often sparse, so fixed preprocessing can both miss critical moments and flood later reasoning with irrelevant content.

Second is capability-driven tool design. Instead of assembling tools heuristically, the authors mine a taxonomy of atomic capabilities from MINERVA expert reasoning traces. They then map these capabilities to 60+ expert tools spanning scripts, VLMs, and specialist models, including overview, temporal localization, OCR, ASR, detection, and face-related recognition. The key point is not the number of tools but the clarity of their boundaries. The paper argues that many video agents fail because tool interfaces are ambiguous, which makes planning and invocation unstable.

Third is the division of labor between a lightweight orchestrator and expert tools. In this setup, the central model is no longer responsible for directly understanding the entire long video. It acts as an adaptive planner and evidence integrator. Once the relevant evidence has been compressed into a short context by tools, even a visually weak or text-centric orchestrator can perform competitively. That is an important systems claim: gains come not only from stronger end-to-end VLMs, but from decomposition, evidence acquisition order, and tool-use policy.

At a higher level, the paper assumes that the main bottleneck in long-video understanding is not single-pass representation capacity alone, but efficient evidence search and intermediate-state management. That is why it chooses an online multi-step agent instead of pushing frame packing further.109:T525,The headline results reported in the paper are 85.1% on Video-MME-Long, 76.5% on LVBench, and 65.7% on MINERVA, using about 50k agent context, including hour-long videos. The authors emphasize that this is achieved with a smaller visual footprint than full-video packing or heavy offline preprocessing, while remaining competitive with frontier systems.

The experiments are designed to support three claims. First, a purely online paradigm is viable: competitive accuracy does not require a prebuilt index. Second, taxonomy-guided tool design matters: performance does not come from arbitrary tool accumulation. Third, strong long-video performance can emerge from agentic tool use rather than only from a very strong native video model.

From the provided content, the likely ablations include online versus offline-then-online pipelines, taxonomy-guided tools versus ad hoc tool sets, orchestrators of different strengths, and accuracy-versus-context-cost comparisons. If those are in the full paper, they are worth checking carefully because they determine whether the method is broadly robust or mainly helps on specific question types.10a:T92e,方法结构很清楚：冻结 actor π_actor，训练 coach π_θ。先让 actor 在输入 x 上生成初始轨迹 y；coach 读取 (x, y)，输出一段自然语言经验 e；然后把 e 作为额外条件，再让同一个 actor 在目标样本 z 上作答，并用 verifier 判断 guided response 是否正确，把这个结果作为 coach 的奖励。关键点有三层。

第一层是奖励设计。same-instance reward 令 z=x，鼓励 coach 做错误诊断、保留有用中间结果、删掉误导性推理；cross-instance reward 则让 z 来自与 x 不同但同任务分布的样本集合 P，迫使 coach 提炼更抽象的任务规则，而不是只写针对单题的补丁。这个区分很重要，因为它把“经验知识”从 case-specific critique 和 transferable strategy 两种形态上拆开了。

第二层是优化方式。作者不是对单个 e 做 REINFORCE，而是对每个源轨迹采样多个候选经验片段，经过 actor rollout 得到组内相对优劣，再用 GRPO 训练 coach。这样做的原因很直接：经验文本质量很难做 token-level 监督，且 reward 只能通过 actor 的最终表现间接观测；组相对优化比单样本高方差策略梯度更稳。

第三层是多轮经验更新。初始 e^(0)=∅，第 k 轮 coach 根据 actor 最新轨迹和已有经验生成更新后的 e^(k)，再让 actor 继续解题。这里不是简单把历史越堆越长，而是“替换式更新”经验表示，让 coach 有机会删除前一轮错误结论、保留已验证信息、补充新发现。这个设计比 naive memory accumulation 更合理，因为原始轨迹里错误会累积，替换式摘要更接近 belief state 更新。

和 self-refinement 的区别在于：self-refinement 直接把原模型的长轨迹或自我批评再喂回原模型，提炼能力仍由 actor 自己承担；L2C 把这件事外包给专门训练过的 coach。和直接 RL 微调 actor 的区别在于：L2C 不改 actor 参数，因此不会轻易破坏 actor 的通用能力，也更适合服务多个冻结 actor 或部署后持续收集经验的场景。论文里还分析了 coach 的 actor-specific 性质：同一个 coach 对不同 actor 的帮助并不完全可互换，说明它学到的不是抽象“正确 critique”，而是“什么样的提示最能让这个 actor 改正”。10b:T8d7,The setup is simple and well scoped. A frozen actor π_actor first produces a trajectory y on input x. A trainable coach π_θ reads (x, y) and outputs a natural-language experience snippet e. The same frozen actor is then prompted with e on a target instance z, and a deterministic verifier scores whether the guided response is correct. That score becomes the reward for the coach.

There are three important design choices.

First, reward variants. With same-instance reward, z=x, so the coach is encouraged to diagnose what went wrong on that specific example and preserve useful intermediate results. With cross-instance reward, z is sampled from a disjoint set of related instances, forcing the coach to extract reusable structure such as task rules or general strategies. This distinction is central: it separates local error correction from transferable experience.

Second, optimization. For each source trajectory, the coach samples multiple candidate experience snippets, each is evaluated through actor rollouts, and the coach is trained with GRPO using relative outcomes within the group. This makes sense because there is no token-level supervision for “good experience,” and the reward is only observable through the actor’s downstream behavior.

Third, iterative experience updating. Starting from empty experience, the coach repeatedly rewrites the current experience after each new actor attempt. The updated experience replaces the previous one rather than simply appending more history. That matters because raw trajectories accumulate errors and irrelevant details; replacement makes the experience representation closer to a belief-state update than to naive memory growth.

Compared with self-refinement, the key difference is division of labor. In self-refinement, the actor must also do the extraction and filtering of its own trajectory. In L2C, that filtering is delegated to a separately trained model. Compared with RL-tuning the actor, L2C preserves the actor’s parameters and broad capabilities, which is attractive for frozen-model deployment settings. The paper also argues that the learned coach is actor-specific: it learns not just what is correct, but what kind of guidance is most effective for that particular actor.10c:T688,The experiments cover mathematical reasoning and interactive text games, which is a sensible pairing: math tests error diagnosis and reuse of intermediate results, while text games test whether the coach can extract latent environment rules from long, noisy interaction histories. Across tasks and model sizes, L2C outperforms the frozen actor, self-refinement, and an untrained coach.

Two findings stand out. First, gains are larger in text games. That is consistent with the method’s premise: when trajectories contain hidden rules and long-horizon evidence, a trained coach has more room to compress useful structure and discard noise. The cross-instance reward is especially helpful when different instances share underlying rules, because it pressures the coach to learn reusable guidance rather than case-specific patches.

Second, iterative coaching behaves like a form of test-time scaling. Performance keeps improving over more iterations with a trained coach, while an untrained coach quickly saturates. On math tasks, allocating extra compute to coach-guided iterations beats simply doubling the actor’s decoding budget. That is an important systems-level result: not all extra inference compute is equally useful, and structured experience extraction can dominate brute-force decoding.

The paper also includes analyses of reward variants, out-of-distribution transfer, and actor-specific transfer. The provided text does not include the full result tables, so it is better not to invent exact numbers, but the evidence structure is clear: task-level comparisons, iteration scaling curves, same-instance vs cross-instance ablations, and transfer analyses.10d:T462,Realtime-Venus contains two separately trained 9B frontend models built on MiniCPM-o 4.5: Realtime-Venus-Omni for audio-visual interaction and Realtime-Venus-Audio for speech-only interaction. The frontend jointly predicts control tokens, response text, and private delegation requests in a streaming sequence. This lets the model learn when to keep speaking through a backchannel, when to stop after a real interruption, when to revise an unspoken continuation, and when to launch background work. The runtime uses a dual-loop design. The conversational model handles live interaction, while Realtime-Venus-Harness executes registered capabilities asynchronously. Each delegation is bound to its original session and committed with the evidence available at the request boundary. Returned results are inserted as private context only after freshness and playback-aware delivery checks, leaving the frontend in charge of the user-facing response. The data pipeline combines scenario planning, speech realization, and temporal alignment, with trajectories for duplex behavior, proactive responses, and delegation workflows.10e:T40a,For pretraining-oriented readers, the main contribution is the training signal design rather than the leaderboard outcome. The Verifiable Experience Pipeline ties tasks, trajectories, tool calls, generated artifacts, and external verification evidence into a single training unit. That is meaningfully different from plain SFT on traces, from RLHF-style preference tuning, and from synthetic agent data that lacks a grounded success criterion. The useful takeaway is threefold. First, it pushes agent training closer to a mid-training or continual-training regime instead of treating tool use as a thin post-training layer. Second, it treats failures as a source for new task construction and environment refinement, which connects naturally to curriculum design, active data construction, and continual pretraining. Third, it studies the development of the model itself as an empirical case of human-agent collaboration. The contribution is better read as a systems-and-paradigm paper than as a fully decomposed, reproducible recipe.10f:T960,The model is built on top of a 744B-parameter MoE foundation model, but the technical center of gravity is the experience pipeline rather than the base architecture.

Step one is grounding each training task in a real execution environment. Instead of only seeing an instruction and a target answer, the model observes environment state, calls tools, inspects outputs, produces intermediate artifacts, and revises its behavior based on feedback. Final outcomes are checked through domain-specific external signals such as executable tests, experiment metrics, file state, geometric checks, source support, or human-defined criteria. This moves supervision away from surface-form imitation toward world-grounded task completion.

Step two is recording a richer training object. A sample is not just prompt-response; it is task + trajectory + artifacts + verification evidence. This matters because it preserves the behavioral chain and the basis for judging success, which should help the model learn when to inspect state, when to invoke tools, and when to recover from failure.

Step three is trajectory curation. The pipeline removes incomplete, contradictory, duplicate, or behaviorally invalid examples. The last category is the interesting one: a trace may look linguistically plausible but still be inconsistent with environment state, produced artifacts, or verification evidence. That is a stronger filter than ordinary text deduplication or heuristic trace cleaning.

Step four is failure-driven task construction. Recurrent failure modes such as poor tool choice, incomplete verification, missing evidence, and failed recovery are used to create new tasks and quality checks. For longer workflows, the recorded experience includes launching jobs, inspecting logs and artifacts, and revising execution plans. The intended effect is to teach transferable debugging and recovery behavior rather than narrow task scripts.

Methodologically, this is not a new RL algorithm and not standard outcome-reward optimization. It is closer to a data engine anchored by external verification, sitting somewhere between agentic mid-training and post-training. Compared with pure outcome supervision, it keeps process information. Compared with pure process distillation, it constrains the process with external results. Compared with online RL, it emphasizes experience construction, filtering, and reuse.110:T804,The empirical section has two parts: capability evaluation on 16 agent benchmarks, and an analysis of the human-agent workflow during the development of Atria Dawn itself.

On benchmark performance, the paper reports evaluation across 16 benchmarks covering tool use, search/research, workspace productivity, professional tasks, software engineering, terminal tasks, ML engineering, and cybersecurity. Atria Dawn Preview is reported as the top score on five benchmarks and second on three more. The currently visible text is more of a results overview than a fully unpacked academic evaluation, so it is difficult to attribute gains cleanly to the base model, the experience pipeline, the tool interfaces, or benchmark protocol differences. One useful signal is that the authors explicitly note uneven performance across domains, which suggests the system is not uniformly strong across all agent settings.

The more informative evidence is the development-process analysis. The paper uses 769 task records from 56 participants, combined with agent logs, to study role allocation. A notable number is that roughly one-third of completed AI-assisted tasks were rated by participants as infeasible without AI under the same scope and resource constraints. The analysis also separates finer roles such as proposing a method, selecting among proposals, diagnosing a difficulty, and executing a revision. The reported pattern is that agents often initiate approaches and carry out changes, while humans concentrate on evaluation, selection, and steering. That is not a standard benchmark result, but it is highly relevant for anyone thinking about recursive improvement loops and agent-assisted model development.

The main empirical limitation is the lack of deeper decomposition in the visible material: data volume, number of experience units, success/failure mix, contribution of different verification channels, and ablations on curation rules are not yet sufficiently exposed. Those details would be necessary to turn the paper into a reusable recipe.111:T559,Read this paper with a training-signal lens rather than a benchmark lens.

Start with the introduction and the Atria Dawn Preview section. The key question is what exactly counts as supervision. The important object is not the 744B MoE base model, but the binding of task, trajectory, artifact, and verification evidence.

Then focus on the Verifiable Experience Pipeline. Three details matter most: what kinds of environment feedback are treated as supervision, what makes an example behaviorally invalid, and how failure cases are converted into new tasks and checks.
